item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q022_colg_crya_remote_homology","answer":"The ColG domain represented by SCOPe domain d1nqda_ from PDB 1nqd and the Cry3A domain-III/C-terminal beta-sandwich represented by d1dlca3 from PDB 1dlc were not treated as a homologous pair in SCOPe 2.04: they were separated below the all-beta class, so the old classification asserted only that both were beta proteins, not that they descended from the same ancestor. In the current SCOPe classification the relationship has been promoted to the superfamily level. They remain in different families, because one family contains clostridial collagenase collagen-binding domains and the other contains Bacillus thuringiensis three-domain Cry-toxin C-terminal receptor-binding domains; the SCOPe change is a remote-homology assignment, not a claim that ColG is a pore-forming Cry toxin or that Cry3A is a collagenase. The supporting evidence is structural first: the isolated ColG collagen-binding domain in 1nqd and the C-terminal domain of Cry3A in 1dlc have the same compact jelly-roll/beta-sandwich core and align in the order and packing of the beta strands despite little detectable pairwise sequence identity. The functional analogy is also at the domain level: both are bacterial extracellular ligand-binding modules appended to larger, unrelated effector proteins, and in both cases the beta-sandwich surface is used for target recognition, collagen binding for ColG versus insect-midgut receptor or glycan binding for Cry3A. That evidence is enough for a SCOPe superfamily placement, but it is too remote for residue-by-residue functional transfer, catalytic annotation transfer, or whole-protein template inference; the shared unit is the C-terminal beta-sandwich binding module only, so 1nqd should be used as the ColG representative and only the d1dlca3/domain-III portion of 1dlc should be used for the Cry3A comparison.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
